We find that models in which stable mass transfer is highly non-conservative and angular momentum is lost as a wind from the donor surface (Jeans mode) maximize the probability of forming dormant systems that match the properties of the observed Gaia BHs in terms of both orbital period and eccentricity, because such assumptions prevent the initial orbit from shrinking too much when the BH progenitor fills its Roche lobe. If we allow for common-envelope evolution, we find that models with common-envelope ejection efficiency $α < 1$ predict dormant systems with orbital periods that are too short compared to the observed Gaia BHs. The eccentricity of the observed Gaia BHs, when combined with information about orbital period and BH mass, favors relatively large natal kicks, similar to those inferred from Galactic neutron stars. Finally, models in which the natal kicks are low - e.g. because they are modulated by fallback - result in the formation of a large population of dormant BHs with long orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb}>10^4$ days) and low eccentricity, which will be tested soon by the fourth Gaia data release.

AI.tldr: This study models formation scenarios of dormant black holes with stellar companions observable by Gaia, finding that non-conservative mass transfer and high natal kicks best match current observations, while future Gaia data will verify predictions about a population formed with low natal kicks and long orbital periods.
AI.motivation: To understand the uncertain formation pathways of dormant black holes (BHs) in binaries detected by Gaia and to predict their properties before the upcoming Gaia data release.
AI.method: Conduct a large parametric study using the population-synthesis code SEVN to simulate isolated binary systems, exploring variables such as accretion efficiency, mass transfer stability, natal kicks, angular momentum transport, and core-collapse supernova models.
AI.result: Models where stable mass transfer is highly non-conservative with angular momentum loss via donor winds (Jeans mode) best reproduce the observed Gaia BH properties. Common-envelope evolution models with low ejection efficiency predict too short orbital periods. High natal kicks explain observed eccentricities and are consistent with neutron star data, while low natal kicks produce many dormant BHs with long orbital periods and low eccentricity anticipated in Gaia's next data release.
AI.conclusion: The formation of dormant Gaia BHs is most consistent with stable, non-conservative mass transfer and significant natal kicks. Future Gaia data will test these predictions, especially the population with long orbital periods and low eccentricities resulting from low natal kicks.

title: High-energy Processes in the Bubbles of Wolf-Rayet Stars: The case of WR 102
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Supersonic winds from massive stars carry great amounts of kinetic power and modify the surrounding interstellar medium. Through this interaction a stellar bubble is formed. Theoretical studies and recent observations suggest that the winds of massive stars could be sources of Galactic cosmic rays. The first detection of synchrotron emission from the bubble of a single star was reported, indicating the presence of relativistic electrons. Studying the non-thermal emission from a single massive star can help to better understand the acceleration of particles taking place in massive star clusters. WR 102 is the perfect case of study. In this work, we present the first high-energy model for the bubble of WR 102: G2.4+1.4. We aim at fitting the radio data and predicting gamma-ray emission. We assume that both electrons and protons are accelerated at the wind shock. We applied a classical model for the stellar bubble and adopted a one-zone model for estimating the radiation produced by the relativistic particles near the acceleration region. Additionally, we computed the expected emission from the protons that diffuse to the outer regions of the bubble. Also, we estimated the leptonic and hadronic contributions expected from cosmic rays. We fitted the observations considering that 3% of the wind kinetic power goes into relativistic electrons, and a magnetic field of 250 $μ$G. The dominant component at high energies is produced by locally accelerated protons reaching the shell. Protons might reach PeV energies in the wind bubble, but the predicted gamma-ray flux is too low to be detectable.

AI.tldr: This study presents the first high-energy emission model for WR 102's stellar bubble, showing particle acceleration up to PeV energies but predicting undetectably low gamma-ray flux despite fitting radio data.
AI.motivation: Understanding particle acceleration in massive star clusters by studying non-thermal emission from a stellar bubble of a single massive star, specifically WR 102.
AI.method: Applied a classical stellar bubble model combined with a one-zone model for radiation from relativistic particles near the acceleration region; considered acceleration of electrons and protons at the wind shock; computed emission from protons diffusing to outer bubble regions; fitted observational radio data using parameters for kinetic power conversion and magnetic field strength.
AI.result: Model fits radio observations assuming 3% of wind kinetic power converts to relativistic electrons and a magnetic field of 250 μG; high-energy emission is dominated by locally accelerated protons reaching the shell; protons may reach PeV energies, but predicted gamma-ray flux is below detection thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Stellar wind bubbles like that of WR 102 can accelerate particles to very high energies, potentially contributing to Galactic cosmic rays, but their gamma-ray emission is too faint for current detection capabilities.
